$comment: Private growth-stage coverage. EVERY figure here is press-reported or estimated — there are no filings. Funding data properly belongs to a licensed source (PitchBook/Crunchbase); this is a best-effort layer with as_of dates and confidence set honestly, and refreshing it is one of the agent pipeline's jobs. Marks are stale the moment a round closes: read post_money WITH last_round_date, always.
confidence_note: Assistant knowledge runs to May 2026; entries dated after that came from live search this session. Treat all valuations as last-priced-round marks, not current fair value.

companies.compute_subsidy_note: Azure commitments run both directions — Microsoft invested, OpenAI committed spend back. Reported margin is not separable from that structure.
Amazon and Google are both large investors and primary compute providers. Enterprise/API weighting makes revenue quality higher than consumer-led peers.
Vertically integrated — owns Colossus and its own generation. Capex is on its own balance sheet rather than rented, which is the opposite trade from its peers.
Runs on customers' own cloud spend, so gross margin is genuinely earned rather than subsidised.
THE compute-arbitrage case. Gross margin is a direct function of model input costs it does not control, set by the same labs it competes with for developer attention.

new_companies.name: Perplexity
new_companies.note: AI search. Distribution deals and browser bundling are the wedge; the bear case is that answer quality is a commodity resold at negative gross margin.
new_companies.compute_subsidy_note: Inference cost per query is the whole unit-economics question, and it is paid to companies that also compete with it.

new_companies.name: Mistral AI
new_companies.note: European frontier lab. Sovereignty positioning and open-weight distribution are the differentiators against far better-capitalised US labs.
new_companies.compute_subsidy_note: ASML's participation is a strategic-supplier investment, an unusually direct silicon-to-model capital link.

new_companies.name: Harvey
new_companies.note: Legal AI for large firms. Workflow depth and firm-level procurement cycles are the moat; the risk is that incumbent legal-research owners bundle the same capability.

new_companies.name: Abridge
new_companies.note: Ambient clinical documentation. Health-system integration and revenue-cycle proof are the moat — the hardest distribution in software, and the stickiest once won.

new_companies.name: Glean
new_companies.note: Enterprise search and agents over internal corpora. Permissions-aware indexing is genuinely hard; the threat is Microsoft bundling the same thing into an existing seat.

new_companies.name: Scale AI
new_companies.note: Data labelling and evaluation. Meta's 49% purchase reframed it from a neutral supplier into a strategically aligned one, which cost it customers among Meta's rivals.
new_companies.compute_subsidy_note: Not a compute story — a neutrality story. A supplier half-owned by one lab is not a supplier the others can use.

new_companies.name: Together AI
new_companies.note: Open-model inference and training cloud. Competes on price per token against both hyperscalers and neoclouds, which is a difficult place to build a moat.
new_companies.compute_subsidy_note: Margin is set by GPU rental cost it does not control. Classic compute arbitrage — real business, structurally capped economics.

new_companies.name: Groq
new_companies.note: Inference-specific LPU silicon plus its own cloud. The bet is that inference workloads justify non-GPU architecture; needs volume to amortise a full silicon programme.

new_companies.name: Cerebras Systems
new_companies.note: Wafer-scale accelerators. Filed to go public; heavy historical revenue concentration in a single Gulf-based customer is the disclosed risk.

new_companies.name: Figure AI
new_companies.note: General-purpose humanoids. Valuation prices a platform outcome against pre-revenue deployment — the widest gap between mark and demonstrated economics on this map.
new_companies.compute_subsidy_note: Nvidia is both investor and silicon supplier — the same vendor-financing pattern as the model labs, applied to robotics.

new_companies.name: Physical Intelligence
new_companies.note: Robot foundation models, hardware-agnostic. Sells the layer that makes other people's robots useful — the picks-and-shovels position in embodied AI.

new_companies.name: Applied Intuition
new_companies.note: Autonomy development tooling for OEMs and defence. Sells to the integrators rather than competing with them, which is why it has real revenue while peers do not.

new_companies.name: Anduril Industries
new_companies.note: Autonomous defence systems sold as products rather than cost-plus programmes. Software margin structure applied to a hardware procurement market.

new_companies.name: Waymo
new_companies.note: The only US robotaxi operating driverless at commercial scale in multiple metros. Per-market unit economics and fleet operations cost, not autonomy capability, are now the binding question.
new_companies.compute_subsidy_note: Alphabet-subsidised on compute, capital and talent. Standalone economics have never been tested.

new_companies.name: Crusoe Energy
new_companies.note: Energy-first AI infrastructure — builds generation alongside compute. Owns the scarce input rather than renting it, which is the differentiated position among neoclouds.
